Definition of Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET)
Malignant tumor composed of small, round blue cells
Aggressive malignancies with varying degrees of neuroectodermal differentiation
May be bone or soft-tissue based

Overview
Ewing sarcoma is part of a family of small, round blue cell tumors of neuroectodermal
origin that occasionally are referred to as the Ewing sarcoma family of tumors. Although
these tumors have a wide spectrum of neural differentiation, they share characteristic
iimmunohistochemical, cytogenetic, and molecular features and respond similarly to
Ewing-based chemotherapy regimens.1 Ewing sarcomas are undifferentiated subtypes;
PNETs are differentiated subtypes. The bone and soft-tissue subtypes have the same
molecular and immunohistochemical profiles2 (Resource 1; Video 1).
Video 1 Decilveo AP, O’Connor I, Wittig JC: Small Round Blue Cell Tumors of Bone: An
Interactive Review [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2017. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/18320__Videos. Accessed July 6,
2021.

Epidemiology
Demographics
Second most common primary malignant bone tumor in children
The male-to-female ratio is 3:2.
Most commonly occurs in lower extremity (41%) and pelvis (26%)
Also may be a soft-tissue sarcoma

Epidemiology
Ewing sarcoma is the second most common primary bone malignancy in children (after
osteosarcoma). It accounts for approximately 10% of all primary malignant bone
tumors3 (Resource 2). Although Ewing sarcoma has been reported in patients of all ages,
it is most commonly diagnosed in individuals in their teenage years, with a median age
at diagnosis of 15 years.1 Studies on Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results
Program data have reported male predominance and an annual incidence of Ewing
sarcoma of 1 case per 1 million for all ages and as high as 10 cases per 1 million in
individuals in their teenage years.3 In addition, Caucasians in the United States are nine
times more likely to be diagnosed than African Americans, indicating an ethnic disparity
(Resource 3).
Ewing sarcoma most often occurs in bone. The most common site is the lower
extremities (41%), followed by the pelvis (26%), chest wall (16%), and upper extremities
(9%). Extraosseous disease has been reported in truncal regions (32%), soft tissues of
extremities (26%), head and neck (18%), and retroperitoneum (16%).2 Pathologic fracture
may be present in as many as 15% of patients.1
Etiology
Cell of origin unknown
Hypothesized to be of neuroectodermal differentiation, with PNET thought to be the
differentiated neural tumor and Ewing sarcoma the undifferentiated variant
Possible mesenchymal stem cell derivation

Classic 11;22 chromosomal translocation (EWS-FLI1 is the fusion gene) in 85% of patients

Etiology
The cell of origin remains controversial. Because of the similarities in morphology,
cytogenetics, and clinical behavior, this family of diseases has been postulated to
originate from a unique mesenchymal stem cell capable of multilineage differentiation.1
Tumors referred to as PNETs typically have greater neuroectodermal differentiation, as
indicated by S-100 positivity, Homer Wright rosettes, or pseudorosettes.2 A shared
characteristic of this family of tumors is the presence of a balanced translocation
involving the EWSR1 gene located on chromosome 22 and members of the ETS
transcription factor family, most commonly FLI1 on chromosome 11.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Pain is the most common symptom reported.
Swelling, stiffness, fever, weight loss, fatigue, and loss of appetite occasionally are present and
nonspecific.
The time from symptoms to diagnosis may be many months.

Patient History
Patients with Ewing sarcoma most often report pain and have an enlarging mass.
Constitutional symptoms may be present and often have associated laboratory
abnormalities; however, these findings are nonspecific. Patients with spine-based lesions
may have bowel or bladder dysfunction, radiculopathy, or myelopathy. Pain may indicate
a pathologic fracture of bony lesions. In the absence of pain, the chief complaint often is
fullness or stiffness. The latency from symptom onset to diagnosis is between 5 and 9
months.2

Physical Examination
Clinical presentation
Swelling, limp, and decreased range of motion are variable.
Frequent fever and occasional erythema (mistaken for infection)
Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, lactate dehydrogenase, and white blood cell count
The most common locations are the pelvis, diaphysis of long bones, and scapula (Figure 1).
Figure 1 Images of a pelvis with Ewing sarcoma. A, AP radiograph of the pelvis demonstrates
an indistinct abnormality in the right supra-acetabular region. B, Technetium-99m bone scan
of the pelvis shows avid uptake in in the right supra-acetabular region. C, Axial MRI of the
acetabular region shows an elevated periosteum. Biopsy was consistent with Ewing sarcoma.
(Reproduced from Weber KL: Malignant bone tumors, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 1560-1586.)
Metastatic disease is found on presentation in 25% of patients.
Staging
Staging workup includes bone marrow biopsy and standard imaging studies (chest CT,
radiography/MRI of the primary lesion, bone scintigraphy/positron emission
tomography/CT).

Physical Examination
A mass or asymmetry frequently is present on physical examination. Erythema may be
present, especially with rapid growth. Regional lymphadenopathy may be present but
does not necessarily indicate nodal disease. Approximately 20% to 28% of patients have

a fever.1 In those patients, leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers are more
commonly noted.
Approximately 25% of patients have detectable metastatic disease at the time of
diagnosis. Staging includes the standard workup for bone sarcomas (plain radiography,
MRI of the whole bone, chest CT, bone scintigraphy/positron emission tomography/CT)
and bilateral bone marrow aspiration and biopsy. All patients are assumed to have
micrometastatic disease. This conclusion was drawn from historical data in which
localized disease was largely managed via amputation, yet disease progression was rapid
and overall survival was low.2
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Purely lytic bone destruction
Periosteal reaction in multiple layers (onion skin) or sunburst pattern (Figure 2, A and B)

Figure 2 Images of an 11-year-old boy. AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of the left tibia and
fibula demonstrate a lesion in the fibular diaphysis. C, Axial, T2-weighted fat-saturated MRI of
the left tibia and fibula shows an extensive soft-tissue mass consistent with a small, round cell
lesion. D, Low-power histologic image shows a small, round blue cell lesion with large sheets of
necrosis. E, Higher-power histologic image shows the monotonous small cells with prominent
nuclei and scant cytoplasm characteristic of Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor.
Needle biopsy was consistent with Ewing sarcoma. The initial periosteal reaction ossified
slightly after two cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. (Reproduced from Weber KL: Malignant
bone tumors, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1560-1586.)
Poorly marginated and permeative
Extensive soft-tissue mass often present despite more subtle bone destruction (Figure 2, C
and Figure 3)

Radiographic differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, osteosarcoma, Langerhans cell
histiocytosis, osteoid osteoma, and lymphoma.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI necessary to identify soft-tissue extension and marrow involvement (Figure 2, C and
Figure 3)
Bone Scintigraphy
Whole-body bone scan can detect skip or distant osseous metastases.
Occurs in 10% of patients.

Ewing sarcoma most often arises from the metaphyseal and diaphyseal regions of the
lower extremity long bones. The typical appearance of these lesions is a permeative
radiolucent destructive intramedullary lesion with a wide zone of transition. An
associated soft-tissue mass is common and may be surprisingly large in relation to the
preserved cortical bone. A laminated or multilayered periosteal reaction, often described
as onion skin appearance, may be present.1
Because plain radiographs may be misleadingly unrevealing, MRI is critical for tumor
localization and for determining soft-tissue mass extent, the presence of skip
metastases, and the relationship to neurovascular structures. Whole-body bone
scintigraphy also is useful for the detection of skip metastases and distant osseous
metastases. Advanced imaging studies, such as these imaging modalities and positron
emission tomography–CT also are useful in assessing tumor response to neoadjuvant
therapies.
Pathology
Gross appearance may be a viscous consistency, mimicking pus.
Small, round blue cells with round/oval nuclei (Figure 2, D and E) and indistinct cell outlines
Prominent nuclei and minimal cytoplasm
Reactive osseous or fibroblastic tissue may be present.
Broad sheets of necrosis and widely separated fibrous strands may be present.
Differential diagnosis includes lymphoma, osteomyelitis, neuroblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma,
Langerhans cell histiocytosis, mesenchymal chondrosarcoma, and leukemia.
Immunohistochemical stains are helpful to identify CD99 positivity (013 antibody).
An 11:22 chromosomal translocation produces EWS-FLI1, which can be identified via
polymerase chain reaction in 85% of patients and differentiates Ewing sarcoma from other
round cell lesions.
Additional features observed only in PNET include a more lobular pattern and arrangement of
the cells in poorly formed rosettes around an eosinophilic material (Figure 4).

Figure 4 High-power histologic image shows a primitive neuroectodermal tumor. Note that the
cells are arranged in a rosette pattern around a central eosinophilic substance. (Reproduced
from Weber KL: Malignant bone tumors, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic
Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1560-1586.)

Pathology
Grossly, the Ewing sarcoma family of tumors may appear variably with necrosis,
hemorrhage, or a cystic appearance. Histologically, the cells are small, round blue cells
with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. The cells have glycogen-rich, scant cytoplasm
that will be positive on periodic acid–Schiff stain. The origin of these neoplastic cells is
unknown but they appear to vary in their differentiation into neuroectodermal or
mesenchymal cell types. The cells may be undifferentiated (Ewing sarcoma) or
differentiated (PNET). The PNET tumors demonstrate features of neural differentiation,
such as Homer Wright rosettes or pseudorosettes.

The differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, lymphoma/leukemia,
rhabdomyosarcoma, neuroblastoma, and eosinophilic granuloma. Molecular pathology
may be useful in determining the diagnosis because an estimated 85% of tumors in the
Ewing sarcoma family express the EWS-FLI1 fusion gene. Several translocations have
been identified and often involve chromosomes 11 and 22. A CD99
immunohistochemical stain often is positive but is nonspecific.1
Management
Techniques/Procedures
Systemic Management
Standard management of Ewing sarcoma is neoadjuvant chemotherapy and surgery/radiation
therapy.
The most common chemotherapy drugs include vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide,
ifosfamide, and etoposide.

Systemic Management
Approximately 25% of patients will have detectable metastatic disease at the time of
presentation; however, all patients are assumed to have micrometastatic disease.
Therefore, current treatment paradigms involve systemic chemotherapy and local
disease control via surgery and/or radiation therapy. Local control decisions depend on
the resectability of the tumor. The Ewing sarcoma chemotherapy regimen involves
vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide, alternating with ifosfamide and
etoposide.2
Local Management
Local control of the primary tumor can be achieved via wide surgical resection or external
beam irradiation.

Most isolated extremity lesions are managed via surgical resection rather than via radiation
therapy because of short-term and long-term adverse effects of radiation therapy and better
potential local control with surgical management (Video 2).
Radiation therapy often is used for the primary lesion in patients who have inoperable tumors
or metastatic disease.
Local control is controversial for localized pelvic Ewing sarcoma and may involve surgical
management and/or radiation therapy.

Local Management
Video 2 Comer BJ, Hayden B, Villalobos CE, Wittig JC: Non-invasive ‘Magnetic’ Distal
Femoral Expandable Endoprosthesis [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2013. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-
page/1718__Videos. Accessed July 6, 2021.
Local disease control can be achieved via wide resection or radiation therapy. Extremity
tumors that are relatively small often are managed surgically, whereas management of
pelvic/truncal and large tumors in which surgical management would result in functional
morbidity has trended toward radiation therapy and/or surgery. A benefit of surgical
resection is the ability to assess treatment response.

Radiation therapy has been used for local disease control in patients in whom surgical
treatment is not possible or would result in unacceptably high morbidity or in whom
positive margins are a concern. Radiation therapy also has been used in patients with
poor response to chemotherapy. The irradiation field should include the pretreatment
volume and an adequate margin. Selection bias has compromised the strength of data in
attempts to elucidate oncologic outcomes based on surgery or radiation therapy1
Complications
Complications of irradiation in skeletally immature patients include joint contractures, fibrosis,
physeal arrest, growth disturbance, limb-length discrepancy, muscle atrophy, pathologic
fracture, and secondary malignancy (usually 10 to 20 years later).
Outcomes
Response to chemotherapy (percent necrosis) is used as a prognostic indicator of overall
survival (>99% necrosis associated with improved survival).
Patients with localized extremity Ewing sarcoma have a 5-year event-free survival of 73%.
Patients with metastatic disease have a poor prognosis (5-year survival <20%).
Metastases occur primarily in the lungs (60%) but also in the bone (43%) and bone marrow
(19%). With recurrent disease, event-free survival is less than 10% at 3 years.
Adverse prognostic factors include non-pulmonary metastasis, less than 90% necrosis, large
tumor volume, and pelvic lesions.
Different EWS-FLI fusion protein subtypes do not predict different outcomes.
PNET is thought to be associated with a slightly poorer prognosis than Ewing sarcoma.

Outcomes
Similar to osteosarcoma, tumor response to chemotherapy has prognostic implications.
In a study of patients with localized disease, progression-free survival (PFS) correlated
with the percentage viability of the resected tumor. Patients with a tumor with less than
5% viability had a 5-year PFS of 75%, whereas patients with a tumor with greater than
30% viability had a 5-year PFS of 20%.4

13/16

Most patients have localized disease, and, with modern treatment paradigms, 5-year PFS
is 70%.5 Metastatic disease remains a negative prognostic factor. If detectable at the
time of diagnosis, mean 5-year survival is 33%.5 Risk factors for metastatic disease at
presentation are older age, axial tumor location, and larger tumors.6
Metastatic disease most commonly occurs in the lungs (60%), followed by bone (43%)
and bone marrow (19%). Patients with osseous disease are more likely to have bone
marrow involvement. Patients with simultaneous pulmonary and osseous involvement
have a poor prognosis. The prognosis for patients with recurrent or metastatic disease is
poor, with overall survival of less than 10%.7
